newsitem.title: USA: NY watchdog sees no hit from part of welfare plan.
newsitem.headline: NY watchdog sees no hit from part of welfare plan.

text.p: The New York state comptroller said he did not expect any adverse effects from part of the new federal welfare reform bill that makes dramatic changes in the program.

"My preliminary analysis indicates that there should be no negative short-term budget impact on New York from the funding formula changes in the Temporary Assistance to Needy Familes and childcare legislation," said H. Carl McCall.
The Temporary Assistance to Needy Families program replaces the Aid to Familes with Dependent Children plan.
McCall, who made the remarks in a letter to New York Gov. George Pataki, estimated that the new program might have a surplus of $250 million to $300 milllion in its first year.

But McCall noted that the the budget advantage will decline in future years, and major decisions to be be made in other areas, such as food stamps, and how legal immigrants will be treated, may undercut its "practical benefit."
Pataki has said the new welfare rules might cause New York to incur hundreds of millions of dollars of new expenses.
The Aid to Families with Dependent Children program was the main federal cash welfare program.
New York is one of the most vulnerable states under the new federal rules, partly because it has a constitutional requirement to help care for the needy.

Further, the state has a large share of the nation's immigrants. The new federal program bars for five years most federal aid, including Medicaid and cash welfare to future legal immigrants. And current immigrants could not get disability and Food Stamps during their first five years in the United States.
